title: Benchmarks
text: Documents splits a value into one {doc}::{field} key per field, and it runs a CBOR encode and decode for each field. These microbenchmarks measure the cost of that work against using raw MMKV directly. The raw baseline encodes the same 5-field value once with CBOR and calls MMKV's byte API. Sample type: @Serializable data class Profile ( val id: Long , val name: String , val email: String , val age: Int , val active: Boolean , )

title: Benchmarks
text: Each raw MMKV baseline does the same underlying work as the Documents call it is paired with. It uses the same field keys, the same per-field CBOR encode and decode calls, the same existence prefix scan before a read, and the same prefix scan and remove on clear. It does all of this by hand, with no library machinery: no lock, no change bus, and no composite encoder. That isolates what the abstraction costs on top of doing the identical raw operations manually. The comparison does not pit Documents' per-field storage against a single whole-object blob, because that would be an unfair comparison. The numbers are captured on a device or simulator. This is not a JVM host benchmark, because MMKV is memory-mapped and needs a real device or simulator. The numbers depend on the device and OS, they are illustrative and not authoritative, and they are not run in CI.

title: Benchmarks
text: Operation Documents Raw MMKV (same work, by hand) set(value) (5 field) 22.3 µs 18.8 µs get (5 field) 20.2 µs 9.1 µs update { } (whole-object, full get+set) 44.2 µs 28.9 µs update(prop, value) (1 field) 3.9 µs 2.3 µs delete (incl. set, 5 field) 23.5 µs 18.8 µs field delegate write (1 field) 5.2 µs 2.3 µs Device: iPhone 17 Pro simulator, iOS 26.1. Median of 20k iterations, CBOR encoding. How to read the table: Whole-object update { } . The builder always does a full 5-field get followed by a full 5-field set, even when only one field changed. This is the read-modify-write path. The raw baseline repeats that same round trip instead of a hand-tuned single-key patch, so the pairing stays honest. update(prop, value) . This is a true single-key write with no read. It is even cheaper than a field delegate write, because it skips the ReadWriteProperty object that the delegate allocates. delete . This measures a set followed by a delete. Absolute timings. They come from a simulator, so they reflect the host CPU and not real hardware. Compare Documents with raw MMKV within this table, and not against other platforms.

title: Benchmarks
text: These numbers are pending a re-run. An instrumented harness already exists ( connectedAndroidDeviceTest , with the same timing harness as iOS). The old numbers were measured before the switch to CBOR, so they need a fresh on-device run before they can be published here. See Field Decomposition for why update(prop, value) and field delegates measure so much cheaper than a whole-object update { } . See Read & Write for when to use each call.

title: Concurrency
text: The document API is synchronous and non-suspending . get() , set() , update() , delete() , exists() , and every field delegate are plain function calls. None of them are suspend functions, and none of them need a coroutine scope. MMKV is memory-mapped, so a read or a write is a memory operation and not disk I/O. There is nothing to wait for. // no coroutine scope needed for any of these: note. set ( Note (title = "Pick up milk" )) val current = note. get () note.update( Note ::done, true )

title: Concurrency
text: Every write to a document goes through a lightweight lock. The lock does not suspend, and it is not a coroutine Mutex . Because it never suspends, it works safely in plain synchronous code and cannot block a coroutine dispatcher in a way that starves other coroutines. The lock is what makes a multi-field update { current -> ... } atomic. Reading the current value and writing the new one happen as one uninterrupted step, so a concurrent reader never sees a half-applied update. The lock belongs to the document's store, not to the Document object you hold. All instances of the same document share it. If two instances update the same document at the same time, one update runs after the other, and neither is lost. Internally, each store has a fixed set of 64 locks. The library picks one by the document's key, and creates it only when it is first needed. Different documents normally get different locks and never wait for each other. Rarely, two unrelated documents map to the same lock, and then their writes take turns.

title: Concurrency
text: Only the collection of flow() and stateFlow() runs on a configurable dispatcher. It is Dispatchers.Default unless you change it, because reading and decoding a value for each change is CPU work (see Reactivity Model ). The dispatcher only affects how a Flow is collected. The document operations themselves stay synchronous, whichever dispatcher your code is running on.

title: Decorations
text: A decoration is a transform from bytes to bytes. It is applied to one field's value after that value has been encoded as CBOR, and it sits between a Document<T> and the storage layer underneath it. It is the mechanism behind FieldDecorator . See Field Decorators for how to attach one.

title: Decorations
text: interface FieldDecorator { fun wrap(fieldName: String , bytes: ByteArray ): ByteArray fun unwrap(fieldName: String , bytes: ByteArray ): ByteArray } wrap runs on every write, right before the encoded bytes reach storage. unwrap runs on every read, right after the bytes come back from storage and before they are decoded. fieldName is the field's own name, such as "title" for Note::title . It is never a raw storage key. A decorator can single out one field with a check like if (fieldName == Note::title.name) ... .

title: Decorations
section: Why reads go in the opposite order
text: When you configure more than one decorator, a write passes through the list from left to right, and a read passes through it from right to left: decorators.fold(bytes) { acc, decorator -> decorator.wrap(fieldName, acc) } // write decorators.foldRight(bytes) { decorator, acc -> decorator.unwrap(fieldName, acc) } // read Think of each decorator as a layer wrapped around the bytes. The last decorator to wrap on a write is the outermost layer, so it has to be the first one removed on a read. Reversing the list on the read side is what makes unwrap undo wrap correctly for any number of decorators. This also means the order you choose matters. With listOf(Compress, Encrypt) , the bytes are compressed first and the compressed result is encrypted. On a read, the data is decrypted first, and then decompressed. If you reversed the pair, the library would try to compress bytes that are already encrypted. Encrypted bytes look random, so they do not shrink.

title: Decorations
section: A sketch of encryption as a decoration
text: Encryption fits this shape well. wrap encrypts the plaintext bytes, and unwrap decrypts them again. Here is a minimal sketch: class EncryptingDecorator ( private val cipher: Cipher ) : FieldDecorator { override fun wrap(fieldName: String , bytes: ByteArray ): ByteArray = cipher.encrypt(bytes, associatedData = fieldName.encodeToByteArray()) override fun unwrap(fieldName: String , bytes: ByteArray ): ByteArray = cipher.decrypt(bytes, associatedData = fieldName.encodeToByteArray()) } Passing fieldName as associated data ties each ciphertext to its own field. If a value is copied from one field's storage key to another's, it fails to decrypt. It does not silently succeed with the wrong field's data. See Session & User State for a complete, working AES-GCM implementation.

title: Decorations
text: If unwrap throws a SerializationException , an IllegalStateException , or an IllegalArgumentException , the failure surfaces as a DocumentDecodingException . See Error Handling .

title: Field Decomposition
text: A document is never stored as one serialized blob. Each top-level field becomes its own MMKV entry, stored under a key of the form {document}::{field} : // Note(title = "Pick up milk", body = "2%, not whole", done = false) // stored as: note- 1 ::title -> bytes note- 1 ::body -> bytes note- 1 ::done -> bytes The :: separator is reserved for this purpose. That is why a document key that contains it is rejected. See Opening Documents .

title: Field Decomposition
text: Decomposition is what makes field-level reactivity and cheap single-field writes possible. update(prop, value) and field delegates each touch exactly one stored key. That is a single putBytes or getBytes call, no matter how many other fields the document has. Nothing else is read or encoded again. update { current -> ... } works differently. It reads and then writes the whole document. Every field is decoded on the read, and every field is encoded and written again on the write, even when the builder changes only one of them. See Read & Write for when to use each form, and Benchmarks for the measured cost difference between the two.

title: Field Decomposition
text: A field whose type is itself a @Serializable object is stored as a single serialized value under that field's key. Examples are a Player inside a save file or an address inside a user profile. This holds at any nesting depth. In v1, nested types are not split up further. Only top-level fields get their own key.

title: Field Decomposition
text: The library finds each type's fields through kotlinx.serialization's SerialDescriptor , never through reflection. That keeps it working the same way on Kotlin/Native (iOS) as on the JVM. A custom encoder and decoder write and read each element under its own {doc}::{field} key, instead of using one shared output buffer. Each field is also where a decoration attaches, if one is configured. A field has one key and one wrap and unwrap pair.

title: Reactivity Model
text: MMKV has no built-in way to listen for changes, so reactivity in Documents is handled entirely inside your process, on top of MMKV.

title: Reactivity Model
text: Each store has one change bus. The default store has one, and so does every named collection. The bus is a stream of events that lives in memory inside your process. After every committed write or delete, the library puts the key of the affected document on the bus. A call to document.flow() listens to the bus and reacts only to events for its own key. When one arrives, it reads the document again and emits the fresh value. Emissions are conflated, which means a burst of quick writes does not pile up redundant emissions. The first value is emitted as soon as collection starts, before any new write has happened. note.flow().collect { current -> // runs once right away with the current value, then again after every committed write } fieldFlow(prop, default) narrows this down to a single field. A change to a sibling field never triggers it. See Field Delegates .

title: Reactivity Model
section: Several instances of the same document
text: The bus belongs to the store, not to the Document object you hold. Every instance opened on the same store uses the same bus. So a write through any instance reaches flow() , stateFlow() , and fieldFlow() on all the others. This works no matter how the instances were created. They can come from dependency injection, from repeated calls to Documents.document(...) , or from separate calls to Documents.collection(name) with the same name. val reader = Documents .document< Note >( "note-1" ) val writer = Documents .document< Note >( "note-1" ) reader.flow().collect { current -> // runs when the write below commits, even though it went through a different instance } writer. set ( Note (title = "Pick up milk" )) Collections are separate stores. The same document key in two collections with different names is two unrelated documents, and a write to one does not notify the other. Each call to Documents.inMemory() also creates its own isolated store.

title: Reactivity Model
text: The change bus only exists inside one process, so changes made by another OS process are not detected. A write from another process never shows up as an emission on this bus. This matches the single-process rule that applies to storage in general. Both the storage and the reactivity are designed for one process that owns each store.

title: Serialization (CBOR)
text: The library uses a single internal CBOR format. It sits between the field walker and the storage layer, and it encodes each field value directly to bytes. There is no JSON text and no intermediate string. // conceptually, per field: val bytes: ByteArray = cbor.encodeToByteArray(serializer, fieldValue) storage.putBytes( "note-1::title" , bytes)

title: Serialization (CBOR)
text: The format is an internal detail, not a setting you can change. The on-disk format is not configurable in v1.

title: Serialization (CBOR)
text: CBOR encodes straight to compact binary. There is no text to produce and no string to parse back, so the format stays small and encoding and decoding stay cheap, on top of a storage engine that is already memory-mapped. Each field is encoded on its own (see Field Decomposition ), so the format only ever has to represent one field's value at a time, never a whole document. If you configure a decoration , it runs right next to this step. It wraps the encoded bytes just after encoding, and unwraps them just before decoding.

title: Storage SPI
text: Under the public API there is a small interface that makes the storage engine swappable. It describes how the library is built. It is not something you implement or configure yourself. internal interface Storage { fun getBytes(key: String ): ByteArray ? fun putBytes(key: String , value: ByteArray ) fun remove(key: String ) fun contains(key: String ): Boolean fun keys(prefix: String ): List < String > } Every stored field key (see Field Decomposition ) is read and written through these five operations. There are two implementations: MmkvStorage wraps a real Tencent MMKV instance. It is used in production on both Android and iOS. InMemoryStorage wraps a plain in-memory map that is safe for concurrent access. It backs Documents.inMemory() , which is used for unit tests that need no real MMKV instance. See Collections & Testing . Everything above this interface lives in commonMain . That includes the public API, field decomposition, serialization, and reactivity. None of it knows which Storage implementation it is talking to. Only the concrete implementation is platform-specific, and that is what keeps the public surface identical across platforms. See Shared KMP Persistence and Platform Support .

title: Contributing
text: Issues, pull requests, and stars all help. The project lives at github.com/nomemmurrakh/documents and is licensed under the Apache License 2.0 .

title: Contributing
section: What a pull request has to pass
text: Every pull request runs through CI, which checks three things: Build and test. iosSimulatorArm64Test runs on macOS, and testAndroidHostTest runs on Ubuntu. ABI check. :documents:checkKotlinAbi guards the public binary surface. Static analysis. detekt checks the Kotlin code.

title: Contributing
text: Significant design decisions are recorded as Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) in docs/adr . To propose a new decision: Open an issue or a pull request that describes the change and why it is needed. Add an ADR file to docs/adr . Name it with the next number in the sequence and a short title, for example 0023-short-title.md . Write it in the same shape as the existing ADRs, with a status, a date, the context, the decision, its consequences, and the alternatives you considered. Add a row for it to the table in docs/adr/README.md . ADRs are numbered in order and are never renumbered or deleted. If a new ADR replaces an older one, the older one stays where it is, and its status is updated to point to the new one.

title: Contributing
text: Read the Guide and Design Decisions to see how the library is built and why. Then open an issue or a pull request on GitHub.

title: Design Decisions
text: This is a curated index of the project's Architecture Decision Records (ADRs). It does not reproduce every one. It groups them by topic and gives each a one-line summary, with a link to the full record.

title: Design Decisions
text: ADR-0004 : Settled on "document" as the user-facing noun. ADR-0007 : Superseded by ADR-0016 An earlier shape for the root factory. ADR-0008 : The update builder returns a new value through copy() instead of changing a receiver. ADR-0016 : Documents is the entry point, and Collection is the handle for a named file. ADR-0017 : Dropped the MergeStrategy enum. The shape of the call now carries the intent. ADR-0018 : update(builder) is the verb, and update(prop, value) writes a single field. ADR-0021 : FieldDecorator is a bytes-in, bytes-out extension point for per-field encryption, compression, or logging.

title: Design Decisions
text: ADR-0001 : Each top-level field gets its own MMKV key. ADR-0003 : Fields are found through SerialDescriptor , never through reflection. ADR-0006 : Superseded by ADR-0015 The earlier per-type Codec design. ADR-0015 : One internal CBOR format replaces the pluggable Codec abstraction.

title: Design Decisions
text: ADR-0002 : Reactivity is built on an in-memory SharedFlow change bus. ADR-0011 : The document API is synchronous with a non-suspending write lock. Only Flow collection is controlled by a dispatcher. ADR-0022 : A process-wide store runtime lets every instance of a document share one change bus and one write lock.

title: Design Decisions
text: ADR-0005 : Publish to Maven Central through macOS CI, not JitPack. ADR-0012 : The library initializes MMKV itself, so you do nothing. ADR-0013 : MMKV is bound on iOS through the Kotlin CocoaPods plugin. ADR-0019 : Dropped multiProcess mode. Storage is always single-process. ADR-0020 : The Kotlin package now matches the Maven groupId.

title: Design Decisions
text: ADR-0009 : Decoding failures surface as DocumentDecodingException . ADR-0010 : field(prop, default) finds its serializer through a reified inline extension. ADR-0014 : Benchmarks run on a device, with a harness native to each platform. For the full history behind any of these, see the complete ADR index on GitHub , or read Contributing to learn how to propose a new one.

title: Collections & Testing
text: A Collection is a named, separate MMKV file. Use one when a group of documents needs its own lifecycle or boundary. Typical reasons are a cache that is wiped on logout, data scoped to one user, or an encryption boundary. See Opening Documents for how to open one.

title: Collections & Testing
text: Documents.inMemory() returns a Collection that behaves the same way but keeps its data in memory instead of a real MMKV file. You need no device and no simulator, and there is no disk state to clean up between tests. Each call to Documents.inMemory() returns its own isolated store, so tests never leak state into each other: val store = Documents .inMemory() val note = store.document< Note >( "note-1" ) note. set ( Note (title = "Test note" )) assertEquals( "Test note" , note. get ()?.title)

title: Collections & Testing
text: Every store can only be used from one process. This applies to the default store, every named collection, and the in-memory backend. See the Overview for the details.

title: Declaring Your Data Class
text: Every Document<T> is backed by an @Serializable class that you write. Each property can be nullable or not, and can have a constructor default or not. Some combinations compile fine but crash at runtime, for example on a button tap. This page explains which ones and how to avoid them.

title: Declaring Your Data Class
text: Documents never invents a value for a field. It only uses one of two sources: a value you already stored, or a default you already declared in the constructor. If neither exists, it fails loudly instead of guessing. There is no correct placeholder the library could make up for a field such as title: String or count: Int . @Serializable data class Note ( val title: String = "" , val count: Int = 0 ) // safe: every field has a default Give every field in a document type either a constructor default or a nullable type ( = null ). A field with neither is only safe if you are certain the document is always written with set() before it is ever changed with update() .

title: Declaring Your Data Class
section: Why this matters: update() on an absent document
text: update { current -> ... } needs a starting value to run the builder on. If the document already exists, that value is the current one. If nothing has ever been written for this key, the starting value is built by decoding the type as if every field were absent. That only works for fields that have something to fall back on: The field has a constructor default , for example val count: Int = 0 . The default is used. This works. The field is nullable and has no default , for example val nickname: String? . It becomes null . This also works, because being nullable is already a fallback. The field is non-null and has no default , for example val title: String . There is nothing to fall back on, so update() throws DocumentDecodingException . The rule is the same for a String , an Int , a nested @Serializable type, or an enum. The library cannot know which value you consider correct for a required field, so it never guesses.

title: Declaring Your Data Class
text: This type looks reasonable and compiles fine: @Serializable data class Note ( val title: String , val count: Int ) // no defaults, both non-null It works perfectly with set() and get() . But if you call update() before the document has ever been written, it crashes. This can happen on the very first button tap in a fresh app install, when you increment a counter: val document = Documents .document< Note >( "note" ) // Crashes if "note" was never set() before: there is no stored title // and no default to fall back to. document.update { it.copy(count = it.count + 1 ) } com.nomemmurrakh.documents.DocumentDecodingException: Cannot update document 'note' because it has not been written yet and field 'title' has no default value. Give 'title' a default in the constructor (`val title: String = ...`), make it nullable (`val title: String?`), or call `set()` with a full value before `update()`. Note The message names the field that needs a default and says how to fix it. Other DocumentDecodingException messages mean something different, such as a damaged value. See Error Handling for what each one means.

title: Declaring Your Data Class
text: Use any one of these: // Give every field a constructor default data class Note ( val title: String = "" , val count: Int = 0 ) // Or make the field nullable, which defaults to null data class Note ( val title: String ?, val count: Int = 0 ) // Or guarantee set() runs before update() ever does document. set ( Note (title = "Untitled" , count = 0 )) document.update { it.copy(count = it.count + 1 ) } // safe now

title: Declaring Your Data Class
text: A field counts as having a fallback in two cases. Either the constructor gives it a default value, or its type is nullable, because null is then a valid fallback. These two options are independent. A non-null field is safe if it has a default, and a nullable field is safe even with no default. Pick whichever reads better for what the field means. See Opening Documents for what else T can and cannot be, and Read & Write for the full picture of get , set , and update .

title: Error Handling
text: get() and field reads throw a DocumentDecodingException when a stored field cannot be decoded. You never get a bare, low-level exception from the serialization layer. try { val current = note. get () } catch (e: DocumentDecodingException ) { log.warn( "note-1 field '${e.field}' failed to decode" , e.cause) } Note In practice this is rare. It only happens if a stored field is genuinely corrupted, or was written by an incompatible older version of your app. You do not need a try / catch around every get() call. Catch it at a boundary that already handles unexpected failures, such as a repository layer or a top-level error handler.

title: Error Handling
text: A document is stored as one MMKV key per field (see Field Decomposition ). So a single field can go bad, for example through a corrupted byte range or a stale format from an old app version, while every other field in the same document stays healthy. DocumentDecodingException tells you which document and field failed: documentKey is the key of the document. field is the field that failed, when there is one. cause is the underlying exception. Without it, the underlying cause would surface as a bare SerializationException , IllegalStateException , or IllegalArgumentException from the CBOR format. Wrapping them means your code catches one library exception type and does not need to know about the serialization layer's own errors. A configured field decorator can fail too. If its unwrap throws one of those three exception types, for example because of a wrong key, corrupted ciphertext, or a failed integrity check, the failure is wrapped in the same way. It looks like any other decode failure.

title: Error Handling
text: A document that was simply never written is not a decoding failure. get() returns null in that case. See Read & Write .

title: Error Handling
text: A DocumentDecodingException has one of four messages. Each one starts differently and says what to do: "Cannot update document 'note' because it has not been written yet…" The first update() ran on a document that was never written, and a field has no constructor default and is not nullable. Give the field a default, make it nullable, or call set() first. See Declaring Data Classes . "Document 'note' is missing a stored value for required field 'title'…" A stored document has no value for a required field. It was probably written by a different version of your data class. Give the field a default or make it nullable so older data still loads. "Field 'title' of document 'note' could not be read as kotlin.String…" The stored bytes are corrupted, or were written by an incompatible version of your data class. "A field decorator failed to unwrap field 'authToken'…" A FieldDecorator threw while reading. Check that the decorators, their order, and any keys match the ones used when the value was written. The last two messages include the name of the underlying exception, such as SerializationException , but not its text. A decoder error can quote stored data, and a stored value must not end up in a log. The full exception is on cause if you need it.

title: Field Decorators
text: A FieldDecorator lets you hook into the read and write path of a document, one field at a time. It can wrap a field's bytes before they reach storage, and unwrap them when they come back. Use it for per-field encryption, compression, checksums, or logging.

title: Field Decorators
text: You can configure decorators on a collection, on a document, or on both: val notes = Documents .collection( "notes" ) { decorators = listOf( LoggingDecorator ()) } val note = notes.document< Note >( "note-1" ) { decorators = listOf( ChecksumDecorator ()) } // note's effective decorator list, in order: [LoggingDecorator(), ChecksumDecorator()] Decorators on a collection apply to every document opened in that collection. Decorators on a document are added after them, for that document only.

title: Field Decorators
text: On a write, the bytes pass through the decorator list from left to right. On a read, they pass through it from right to left. The decorator that ran last on write runs first on read, so each wrap is undone in the reverse of the order it was applied: // decorators = listOf(Compress, Encrypt) // write: bytes -> Compress.wrap -> Encrypt.wrap -> stored // read: stored -> Encrypt.unwrap -> Compress.unwrap -> bytes This is why you should compress first and encrypt second, and not the other way around. Encrypted bytes look random, so they do not compress in any useful way. See Decorations for why the library applies the list in this order.

title: Field Decorators
text: Decorators also apply to field delegates. See Field Delegates . Decorators run right next to where CBOR encoding and decoding happen. See Serialization (CBOR) and Field Decomposition . If a decorator's unwrap fails, the failure surfaces as a DocumentDecodingException , the same as any other decode failure. See Error Handling .

title: Field Delegates
text: Sometimes you do not need the whole document. You only want one field, read and written like an ordinary Kotlin property. Field delegates give you that while keeping the storage typed and reactive. class NoteEditor { private val note = Documents .document< Note >( "note-1" ) var done: Boolean by note.field( Note ::done, default = false ) val doneFlow: Flow < Boolean > = note.fieldFlow( Note ::done, default = false ) }

title: Field Delegates
text: field(prop, default) returns a ReadWriteProperty that is backed by a single stored key. Reading it returns default if the field was never set. Writing it updates only that field's key and leaves the rest of the document alone. A write also emits on the document's flow() : editor.done = true // writes only the "done" field's key println(editor.done) // reads only that key

title: Field Delegates
text: A property's declared default value cannot be recovered from a KProperty at runtime. Once you hold a bare property reference, there is no way to ask what default the data class gave it. So field() and fieldFlow() both take default as an explicit argument.

title: Field Delegates
text: On collection, fieldFlow emits the current field value, or default if the field was never set. After that it emits a new value each time that field changes. A change to a sibling field does not trigger it: note.fieldFlow( Note ::done, default = false ).collect { done -> checkbox.setChecked(done) }

title: Field Delegates
text: If you only need a one-off write to a field and have no property to declare, call note.update(Note::done, true) . It does the same single-key write directly. See Read & Write . Use it in code that does not own a var property backed by the field.

title: Field Delegates
text: field() and fieldFlow() read and write through the same internal path as update(prop, value) , so any configured FieldDecorator s run here as well. See Field Decorators .

title: Field Delegates
text: Field delegates suit settings-style code: a screen with a handful of independent toggles or values, each bound directly to a property, where you never need to read or write the rest of the document. See Settings & Preferences for a fuller example.

title: Guide
text: These guides walk through the public API one task at a time. Start here if you want the full picture and not just the quick tour. Opening Documents : documents and collections, opening the same document more than once, and why there is no setup step. Declaring Data Classes : when to use a nullable type or a constructor default, and a first-run crash to avoid. Read & Write : set , update , and single-field update , and when to use each. Reactivity : flow() and stateFlow() , with a snippet for Compose. Field Delegates : binding a single field with by , without touching the whole document. Field Decorators : transforming the bytes of a field, for example to encrypt or compress it. Collections & Testing : separate MMKV files, the in-memory backend for tests, and the one-process rule. Error Handling : what happens when a stored field cannot be decoded.

title: Opening Documents
text: Documents is the entry point. You can open a document directly on the default store, or open a named Collection first when a group of documents needs its own MMKV file.

title: Opening Documents
text: Documents.document<T>(key) is the common case. It gives you the document stored under key in the default store, and it needs no configuration: @Serializable data class Note ( val title: String = "" , val body: String = "" , val done: Boolean = false ) val note = Documents .document< Note >( "note-1" ) Opening a document does not write anything. It only gives you a handle to whatever is stored under that key, so note.get() returns null until something has been written. You can pass an optional configuration block. It has two settings: dispatcher is the dispatcher used to collect flow() and stateFlow() . See Reactivity . decorators is a list of FieldDecorator s applied to every field of this document. See Field Decorators . val note = Documents .document< Note >( "note-1" ) { dispatcher = Dispatchers . Default // this is already the default }

title: Opening Documents
text: Use Documents.collection(name) only when a group of documents needs its own file. Typical reasons are a cache that is wiped on logout, data scoped to one user, or an encryption boundary: val drafts = Documents .collection( "drafts" ) { dispatcher = Dispatchers . Default } val draft = drafts.document< Note >( "draft-1" ) Every collection, including the default store, can only be used from one process. See Collections & Testing for details.

title: Opening Documents
section: Opening the same document more than once
text: When it is practical, keep a single instance of a document and share it. Dependency injection is a good way to do that. It is not required, though. Opening a document is cheap, and all instances of the same document on the same store behave as one document: A write through one instance shows up in flow() on the others. If two instances call update at the same moment, the changes are applied one after the other, so neither is lost. So your data stays correct even if two parts of your app open the same document separately. The Reactivity Model explains how the instances stay in sync. Each instance has its own configuration. The dispatcher can differ between instances. Use the same decorators for every instance of a document, because the bytes written by one instance must be readable by the others.

title: Opening Documents
text: T must be a @Serializable class, an enum, or a primitive. It cannot be a top-level List or another collection type. Each stored value is keyed by one of the type's declared properties (see Field Decomposition ), and a bare list has no properties. Opening Documents.document<List<T>>(key) throws DocumentDecodingException immediately. A list works correctly as a field inside a class, so wrap it: @Serializable data class QueueState ( val items: List < OfflineQueueItem > = emptyList()) val queue = Documents .document< QueueState >( "pending-requests" ) See Declaring Data Classes for which fields need a constructor default or a nullable type to stay safe under update() .

title: Opening Documents
text: Internally, every document is split into one stored key per field, named {document}::{field} (see Field Decomposition ). Because :: is reserved for this, a document key that contains it is rejected with an IllegalArgumentException . Choose ordinary identifiers such as "note-1" or "user" .

title: Opening Documents
text: MMKV initializes itself the first time it is needed. On Android this happens through androidx.startup , and on iOS through an internal call that uses the app's sandbox path. You never call MMKV.initialize() and never pass a Context . The first call to Documents.document(...) or Documents.collection(...) is enough. Note On Android, this relies on a <provider android:name="androidx.startup.InitializationProvider"> entry that is merged into your app's manifest. Leave it alone. If you remove or override it, for example with a conflicting tools:node="remove" , MMKV stops initializing and document access fails at runtime.

title: Reactivity
text: A document exposes its changes as a Flow . Your UI, or any other code, can react every time the stored value changes. There is no polling and no need to read the value again yourself. note.flow(): Flow < Note ?> // cold: the current value, then every committed write note.stateFlow(scope): StateFlow < Note ?> // hot: shared while there are subscribers

title: Reactivity
text: flow() is cold, so nothing happens until you collect it. When you do, it gives you the current value straight away, and then a fresh value after each committed write. Rapid writes are conflated, so you may see only the latest value. A write to a different document does not wake this flow up. When the document is deleted, the flow emits null : note.flow().collect { current -> editor.render(current) }

title: Reactivity
text: stateFlow(scope) is hot. It needs a CoroutineScope , and it holds the latest value so you can read it at any time. While at least one collector is subscribed, all of them share the same stream. This suits a stream owned by a ViewModel that should outlive any single collector.

title: Reactivity
text: val current by note.flow().collectAsStateWithLifecycle(initialValue = note. get ()) current is nullable. A value of null means the note has not been written yet.

title: Reactivity
section: How it works under the hood
text: MMKV has no built-in way to listen for changes, so reactivity is handled inside your process. Every store has one change bus. After each committed write or delete, the library puts the affected document's key on that bus. flow() listens for its own key and reads the document again when it sees it. The bus belongs to the store, so separate instances of the same document stay in sync. See Reactivity Model for the full mechanism. It also explains why changes made by another process are not detected.

title: Read & Write
text: There are three ways to write a document, and each has a different purpose. Knowing which one to use is the main thing to learn about this API. note. get (): Note ? // current value, or null if absent note. set (value) // replace the whole document note.update { current -> ... } // build a new value from the current one (or the defaults) note.update( Note ::done, true ) // single-field update: writes just that key, no read note.delete() // remove the document and all its field keys note.exists(): Boolean // true if any field key is stored

title: Read & Write
text: get() returns the current value, or null if the document has never been written. A missing document is not an error: val current: Note ? = note. get ()

title: Read & Write
text: Pass a complete object and it replaces the whole document, including every field whether it changed or not: note. set ( Note (title = "Pick up milk" , body = "2%, not whole" ))

title: Read & Write
text: The builder receives the current value as the current parameter and returns a new value built with copy() . If the document has not been written yet, current holds the type's defaults. This has the same shape as MutableStateFlow.update { current -> ... } in kotlinx.coroutines. Fields you do not touch keep the value they had: note.update { current -> current.copy( title = "Pick up oat milk" , body = "The barista-approved kind" , ) } This reads and then writes while holding the document's write lock. A multi-field update is therefore atomic, and a concurrent reader never sees a half-applied write.

title: Read & Write
text: When only one field needs to change, update(prop, value) writes just that field directly. It does not read the rest of the document: note.update( Note ::done, true ) Choose between the two forms of update like this: Use update(prop, value) when you change exactly one field and the new value does not depend on the current one. Use update { current -> ... } when an edit touches more than one field together, or when the new value depends on the current one.

title: Read & Write
text: note.delete() // removes the document and all its field keys println(note.exists()) // false

title: Read & Write
text: Concurrency explains how the write lock keeps a multi-field update atomic. Field Delegates shows how to bind a single field as a property instead of calling update(prop, value) directly. Field Decorators covers how every operation on this page passes through any configured FieldDecorator s, which wrap the bytes on the way to storage and unwrap them on the way back.

title: Documents
text: What's new in v0.2.0 Version 0.2.0 makes it safe to open the same document in more than one place. In v0.1.0, a write was only seen by the instance that made it, so every part of an app had to share a single instance. Sharing a single instance is no longer required, but it is still the recommended approach when it is practical. Instances stay in sync. A write through one instance now reaches flow() , stateFlow() , and fieldFlow() on every other instance of the same document. This holds whether the instances come from dependency injection, from repeated Documents.document(...) calls, or from separate Documents.collection(name) calls. Updates are not lost. If two instances of the same document call update at the same time, both changes are applied one after the other. Clearer error messages. Each cause of a DocumentDecodingException now has its own message that says what went wrong and how to fix it. Nothing to change in your code. The public API is the same as in v0.1.0. Opening Documents explains how to open the same document more than once. The Reactivity Model explains how the instances stay in sync.

title: Documents
text: Documents gives you typed, reactive documents on top of MMKV. You define a data class, treat it as a document, and get typed reads, copy-style updates, and Flow reactivity. It is fast, and it is pleasant to write. @Serializable data class Note ( val title: String = "" , val body: String = "" , val done: Boolean = false ) val note = Documents .document< Note >( "note-1" ) // one call, you have a document note. set ( Note (title = "Pick up milk" , body = "2%, not whole" )) note.update( Note ::done, true ) // one field, no read note.update { current -> // several fields, one atomic write current.copy( title = "Pick up oat milk" , body = "The barista-approved kind" , ) } note.flow().collect { editor.render(it) } // the editor reacts to every write

title: Documents
text: MMKV is extremely fast. It is memory-mapped and about as quick as anything on the platform. Out of the box, though, it only gives you raw keys and primitive values. Every typed object means writing your own serialization and key management again. The typed and reactive alternatives give up that speed in exchange for comfort, so you usually have to choose between fast and pleasant to use. Documents does not make you choose. It puts a clean, idiomatic Kotlin API directly on top of MMKV: typed documents, property delegates, a copy() -style update, and Flow reactivity. The cost is a little CPU for serialization and never any extra I/O. Clean code on top, MMKV all the way down.

title: Documents
text: Android and Kotlin Multiplatform apps often need to store one record of structured data, such as a logged-in user, a settings object, a session, or a draft. None of the usual tools fit this well: SharedPreferences is key-value only, awkward for nested objects, and loads the whole file into memory. Jetpack DataStore is typed, but Proto needs schema files and Preferences is still flat key-value. That is a lot of ceremony for one object. SQLite and Room are relational and table-oriented, which is overkill for a single document with no relations. Raw MMKV is very fast but has no abstraction. Serialization and key management are up to you. No library offered a document-oriented, typed, reactive API with MMKV's performance underneath. Documents is that library.

title: Documents
text: A document-oriented API: get , set , update , delete , exists , flow , and stateFlow . Typed persistence for any @Serializable class, with no per-type boilerplate. Reactivity. Observers are notified when a document or a single field changes. MMKV-class performance. The abstraction adds CPU and memory cost only, never extra I/O. A public API that lives entirely in commonMain , with only the storage engine bound per platform. Internal serialization to a compact CBOR format, with no schema to maintain. A FieldDecorator hook for per-field encryption, compression, or logging. See Field Decorators .

title: Documents
text: Every store is single-process. This includes the default store, every named collection, and the in-memory test backend. Concurrent access to the same store from more than one OS process is not supported and can corrupt it. On Android, a Service runs in your app's own process unless its manifest entry sets android:process , so an ordinary service is safe. A component with android:process , or an iOS app extension such as a widget or a share extension, runs in a separate process. Documents does not set up MMKV there, and if two processes write the same store, updates can be silently lost. This is a firm limit, not an edge case. If your app needs to share a store across processes, this library is not the right fit for that store today. Either design around a single owning process for each store, or keep the multi-process data out of Documents .

title: Documents
text: Installation : add the dependency. No setup is needed. Quick Start : the whole API in one short walkthrough. Guide : task-oriented walkthroughs of every part of the API.

title: Installation
text: com.nomemmurrakh:documents is published on Maven Central. Add it to the commonMain source set of a Kotlin Multiplatform module, or to a plain Android module: // build.gradle.kts dependencies { implementation( "com.nomemmurrakh:documents:0.2.0" ) } iOS: linking MMKV On iOS, your app also needs to add MMKV to its own target, through CocoaPods or Swift Package Manager, the same way as any other native dependency. If it is missing, the build fails with a link error. See Troubleshooting for details.

title: Installation
text: The library initializes MMKV for you the first time it is used. On Android this happens through androidx.startup . On iOS it happens through an internal initializeMMKV call that uses the app's sandbox path. You never call MMKV.initialize() and never pass a Context . Add the dependency, call Documents.document(...) , and you are done. Note On Android, this works because a <provider android:name="androidx.startup.InitializationProvider"> entry is merged into your app's manifest. You do not need to add anything yourself. Just do not remove or override that entry, for example with a conflicting tools:node="remove" that targets InitializationProvider . If you do, MMKV does not initialize and document access fails at runtime.

title: Installation
text: Android and iOS ( arm64 and simulatorArm64 ) are supported today. See Platform Support for the full table and for how MMKV is bound on each target. Continue to Quick Start →

title: Platform Support
text: Platform Status Storage engine Android ✅ MMKV iOS ( arm64 and simulatorArm64 ) ✅ MMKV How the library is configured On Apple targets, MMKV is bound through the Kotlin CocoaPods plugin. Both platforms share one public API, and all of it lives in commonMain . On both platforms the library initializes MMKV itself, so you have nothing to set up for it. There is no JVM, desktop, or wasm target in this release. See Shared KMP Persistence for what this means in practice.

title: Quick Start
text: This walkthrough covers the whole flow in one place. There is no schema, no DAO, and no serialization code to write by hand. The example is a single offline note, the kind of "continue where you left off" document this library is built for.

title: Quick Start
text: Start with an @Serializable data class: import com.nomemmurrakh.documents. Documents import com.nomemmurrakh.documents.document import kotlinx.serialization. Serializable @Serializable data class Note ( val title: String = "" , val body: String = "" , val done: Boolean = false , )

title: Quick Start
text: Opening a document takes one call and no configuration: val note = Documents .document< Note >( "note-1" )

title: Quick Start
text: Use set when you have a complete value, for example when you create the note for the first time: note. set ( Note (title = "Pick up milk" , body = "2%, not whole" ))

title: Quick Start
text: Use update(prop, value) to change a single field. It writes only that one key and does not read the rest of the note: note.update( Note ::done, true )

title: Quick Start
text: Use update { current -> ... } to edit more than one field at once. The builder receives the current value and returns a new one with copy() . Fields you do not touch, such as done here, keep their values: note.update { current -> current.copy( title = "Pick up oat milk" , body = "The barista-approved kind" , ) } println(note. get ()) // Note(title=Pick up oat milk, body=The barista-approved kind, done=true) note.delete() println(note.exists()) // false

title: Quick Start
text: get() returns null if the document has never been written. The three ways to write have different purposes: set(value) replaces the whole document. update(prop, value) writes a single field and does not read anything first. update { current -> ... } reads the current value, or the type's defaults if nothing is stored, and writes back a new one. The read and the write happen atomically, so use it for edits that touch more than one field together.

title: Quick Start
text: Opening Documents : documents and collections, and the automatic MMKV setup. Read & Write : the full difference between set , update , and single-field update . Reactivity : flow() and stateFlow() , with a snippet for Compose. Field Delegates : binding a single field without touching the whole document.

title: Sample App
text: A runnable Compose Multiplatform sample lives in the repository's sample/ folder. It runs on both Android and iOS. It is made of three parts: sample/shared/ holds one shared UI and the business logic for both platforms. sample/androidApp/ is a thin Android wrapper. sample/iosApp/ is a real Xcode project that embeds the shared Kotlin framework through Gradle's embedAndSignAppleFrameworkForXcode task. The sample itself does not use CocoaPods.

title: Sample App
text: A home screen lists six screens. Each one is a real, working screen backed by the real Documents API: Settings & Preferences. Typed, observable app settings. A SettingsRepository wraps Documents.document<AppSettings>("app-settings") and uses the field() and fieldFlow() delegates for theme (SYSTEM, LIGHT, or DARK) and locale . Changing either one is saved instantly and updates the screen's own live readout, with no manual refresh. Session & User State. Signing in and out, with an encrypted auth token. A SessionRepository opens Documents.collection("session") , which is configured with a real FieldDecorator ( AesGcmFieldDecorator , using AES-GCM from cryptography-kotlin ) that wraps authToken . The "Prove authToken is encrypted at rest" action opens a second document with a different AES key and shows the decrypt failure. This is concrete proof that the stored bytes are ciphertext and not the plaintext token. Caches & Drafts. A draft that survives a relaunch, kept in its own store. A CacheRepository opens Documents.collection("cache") , which holds SyncState and DraftPost . The draft text field saves on a debounce and restores when you open the screen. A check on the same screen shows that the theme value from the Settings screen, which is in a different collection, stays untouched when "Clear cache" runs. Reactive UI State. A simulated download that drives a live progress bar. A coroutine ticker repeatedly calls update(DownloadState::bytesDownloaded, bytesSoFar) . A LinearProgressIndicator re-renders only because it collects the document's flow() . There is no polling, and the progress bar does not know where the write came from. Shared KMP Persistence. One offline queue, with identical code on both platforms. A PendingRequestQueue wraps Documents.document<QueueState>("pending-requests") . The queue's items live inside a small wrapper class and not in a bare List document. See Opening Documents for why. The screen has "Enqueue mock request" and "Clear queue" actions and a live list. All of its code is in commonMain . Nothing platform-specific was written to make it work on both Android and iOS. Shared Instances. Two instances of one document, kept in sync. The screen is split into two sections. Each opens its own instance with Documents.document<SharedNote>("shared-note") and collects its own flow() . Pressing "+1" or setting the title in one section updates the other right away. A line on the screen shows that the two instances are different objects ( instanceA === instanceB is false ). "Add 100 from both" runs 100 updates on each instance at the same time, and the count goes up by exactly 200, so no update is lost.

title: Sample App
text: Clone the repository, then follow the steps for your platform: Android. Run the sample/androidApp module from Android Studio or with Gradle. iOS. Open sample/iosApp/iosApp.xcodeproj in Xcode and run it. See Use Cases for the documented pattern that each screen demonstrates.

title: Troubleshooting
text: This page lists common build and runtime errors, and what they usually mean.

title: Troubleshooting
text: Undefined symbol: _OBJC_CLASS_$_MMKV Cause. Your iOS app links the Documents framework, but it has not declared MMKV as a dependency of its own target. Documents depends on MMKV, but embedding the Documents framework does not bring MMKV's native binary along with it. Fix. Add MMKV directly to your app, through CocoaPods or Swift Package Manager, the same way you add any other native dependency. MMKV's own iOS setup guide covers both options.

title: Troubleshooting
section: Crash on the first update() call: DocumentDecodingException
text: DocumentDecodingException: Cannot update document 'note' because it has not been written yet and field 'title' has no default value. Give 'title' a default in the constructor (`val title: String = ...`), make it nullable (`val title: String?`), or call `set()` with a full value before `update()`. Cause. This is the most common surprise the first time you run the library, and it has nothing to do with corrupted data. It happens when update() runs on a document that has never been written with set() , and at least one field in your @Serializable data class is both non-nullable and has no constructor default. An example is data class Note(val title: String, val count: Int) . Nothing is stored yet and there is no default to fall back on, so the library has no value to start that field with. It throws an exception instead of guessing. The message names the field and the fix. A DocumentDecodingException can also mean something else, such as a damaged value or a failing decorator. See Error Handling for what each message means. Fix. Give every field either a constructor default or a nullable type: data class Note ( val title: String = "" , val count: Int = 0 ) See Declaring Data Classes for the full rule and more examples.

title: Caches & Drafts
text: Caches and drafts include the last synced payload, an in-progress form, and the "continue where you left off" data. This data is useful but disposable. Keep it apart from durable settings, so it is easy to reason about and easy to wipe on its own. @Serializable data class SyncState ( val lastSyncedAtEpochMs: Long = 0 , val lastSyncedEtag: String = "" , ) @Serializable data class DraftPost ( val title: String = "" , val body: String = "" , ) val cache = Documents .collection( "cache" ) val syncState = cache.document< SyncState >( "sync-state" ) val draft = cache.document< DraftPost >( "compose-draft" ) The compose screen writes to draft after each debounced keystroke. On the next launch it reads the draft back, so the user continues exactly where they left off: draft.update { current -> current.copy(body = textField.value) } // next launch val restored = draft. get () ?: DraftPost () cache is its own collection, which means it has its own MMKV file. If you reset it, for example from a "reset cache" action or a storage cleanup, by deleting its documents, the durable data in the default store or in another collection is not touched. See Collections & Testing for how collections keep one set of documents separate from another.

title: Use Cases
text: These are five common situations where an app needs one typed, reactive document. Each page walks through a realistic example and links back to the Guide pages that cover the details. Settings & Preferences : the job that SharedPreferences and NSUserDefaults usually do, with typed values you can observe. Session & User State : the signed-in user, auth tokens, and the active profile. Caches & Drafts : the last synced payload, in-progress form drafts, and "continue where you left off." Reactive UI State : any state that Compose or SwiftUI should re-render on. Shared KMP Persistence : one storage API in shared code that runs on both Android and iOS.

title: Reactive UI State
text: Reactive UI state is any state that Compose or SwiftUI should re-render when it changes. A document's flow() gives your UI layer exactly that, with no manual re-reads and no polling. @Serializable data class DownloadState ( val bytesDownloaded: Long = 0 , val totalBytes: Long = 0 , val isComplete: Boolean = false , ) val download = Documents .document< DownloadState >( "active-download" ) A background worker updates bytesDownloaded as chunks arrive. This is a single field, so update(prop, value) is the natural fit. It makes one direct write to that key: download.update( DownloadState ::bytesDownloaded, bytesSoFar) A Compose screen collects the same document and redraws on every write. It does not need to know where the write came from. The screen can even hold a different instance of the document than the worker does, and it still sees every write: @Composable fun DownloadProgressBar (download: Document < DownloadState >) { val state by download.flow().collectAsStateWithLifecycle(initialValue = download. get ()) val progress = state?.let { it.bytesDownloaded.toFloat() / it.totalBytes } ?: 0f LinearProgressIndicator (progress = progress) } The sample app shows this pattern from start to finish. A button press writes to a document, and a separate readout re-renders only because it collects the document's flow() . See Reactivity for the full flow() and stateFlow() API.

title: Session & User State
text: Session state is the signed-in user, an auth token, and the active profile. It belongs to a login session, not to the app's long-lived settings. Keep it in its own collection so it stays separate from data that should survive a logout. @Serializable data class Session ( val userId: String , val displayName: String , val authToken: String , ) val sessionStore = Documents .collection( "session" ) val session = sessionStore.document< Session >( "current" ) // sign in session. set ( Session (userId = "u_42" , displayName = "Mara" , authToken = "…" )) // react to sign-in / sign-out anywhere in the UI session.flow().collect { current -> isSignedIn = current != null } Signing out means deleting the session document. The public API has no "clear the whole collection" call, so sign-out is an explicit delete() on each document that should end with the session: fun signOut() { session.delete() }

title: Session & User State
text: The authToken is a good candidate for field-level encryption, and the session collection is a natural encryption boundary. FieldDecorator is the extension point for this. The example below uses cryptography-kotlin ( dev.whyoleg.cryptography , v0.6.0). It is one choice among several, and your app adds it as a dependency. Documents does not pull it in: // build.gradle.kts (your app/module, not Documents itself) implementation( "dev.whyoleg.cryptography:cryptography-core:0.6.0" ) implementation( "dev.whyoleg.cryptography:cryptography-provider-optimal:0.6.0" ) import dev.whyoleg.cryptography. CryptographyProvider import dev.whyoleg.cryptography.algorithms. AES class AesGcmFieldDecorator ( private val key: AES . GCM . Key , ) : FieldDecorator { private val cipher = key.cipher() override fun wrap(fieldName: String , bytes: ByteArray ): ByteArray = cipher.encryptBlocking( plaintext = bytes, associatedData = fieldName.encodeToByteArray(), ) override fun unwrap(fieldName: String , bytes: ByteArray ): ByteArray = cipher.decryptBlocking( ciphertext = bytes, associatedData = fieldName.encodeToByteArray(), ) } val provider = CryptographyProvider . Default val key = provider. get ( AES . GCM ).keyGenerator().generateKeyBlocking() val sessionStore = Documents .collection( "session" ) { decorators = listOf( AesGcmFieldDecorator (key)) } val session = sessionStore.document< Session >( "current" ) A few details in this example are worth knowing: Blocking calls. The example uses encryptBlocking and decryptBlocking , not the suspending encrypt and decrypt , because FieldDecorator.wrap and unwrap are synchronous. Tamper detection. encryptBlocking puts the nonce and the authentication tag into the returned ByteArray . If a stored value is tampered with or corrupted, AES-GCM detects it instead of decoding garbage. Associated data. Passing fieldName as associated data means a ciphertext copied from one field's key to another fails to decrypt. It does not silently succeed with the wrong data. Keys are your job. Your app is responsible for generating, storing, and rotating keys. The cryptography-kotlin docs cover that part. To see how the extension point itself works, read Decorations and Field Decorators . See Opening Documents for when to use a named collection instead of the default store. Also remember the single-process rule , which applies to every store, including this one.

title: Settings & Preferences
text: Settings are the job that SharedPreferences and NSUserDefaults usually do: theme, locale, feature flags, and onboarding state. Here they are typed and observable, instead of a flat bag of string keys. @Serializable enum class Theme { SYSTEM , LIGHT , DARK } @Serializable data class AppSettings ( val theme: Theme = Theme . SYSTEM , val locale: String = "en-US" , val hasCompletedOnboarding: Boolean = false , ) class SettingsRepository { private val doc = Documents .document< AppSettings >( "app-settings" ) var theme: Theme by doc.field( AppSettings ::theme, default = Theme . SYSTEM ) var locale: String by doc.field( AppSettings ::locale, default = "en-US" ) val themeFlow: Flow < Theme > = doc.fieldFlow( AppSettings ::theme, default = Theme . SYSTEM ) } Each setting reads and writes like an ordinary property. Changing theme touches only that field's key. themeFlow lets your UI update as soon as the theme changes, with no polling and no need to read the rest of the settings object. See Field Delegates for how field() and fieldFlow() work.

title: Shared KMP Persistence
text: With one storage API in commonMain , the same document code runs unchanged on Android and iOS. Each platform keeps its own data in MMKV, and your shared code does not need to know which platform it is on. // commonMain @Serializable data class OfflineQueueItem ( val id: String , val endpoint: String , val payloadJson: String , val attempts: Int = 0 , ) @Serializable data class QueueState ( val items: List < OfflineQueueItem > = emptyList(), ) class PendingRequestQueue { private val doc = Documents .document< QueueState >( "pending-requests" ) fun enqueue(item: OfflineQueueItem ) { doc.update { current -> current.copy(items = current.items + item) } } fun observe(): Flow < List < OfflineQueueItem >> = doc.flow().map { it?.items ?: emptyList() } } The queue is wrapped in a QueueState class. It is not opened directly as Documents.document<List<OfflineQueueItem>>("pending-requests") , because a top-level List is not supported as a document type today. Each stored value is keyed by one of the class's declared properties, and a bare list has none. A list works correctly as a field inside a @Serializable class, as shown here. See Opening Documents for the full rule. PendingRequestQueue is written once, in commonMain . An Android ViewModel and an iOS view model use it in exactly the same way. You write no platform-specific persistence code and have nothing to keep in sync, because the whole public API and its logic live in commonMain . Only the underlying Storage implementation differs per platform, and that is an internal detail the library handles. See Storage SPI and Platform Support for how each target is bound.
